title: Do you actually write a massive GDD, or do you wing it as you build?
author: ninjasaid13
selftext:
Curious how people here handle the planning stage.

Do you map out a comprehensive game design document covering every system, mechanic, and balance sheet before touching code? Or do you start with a rough core loop and figure out the rest while prototyping?

If you do write documentation, how detailed do you get before it starts feeling like busywork?

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body: The more detailed you can be at the start, the better the development will be and the less you'll spend in refactoring shit.

comments.author: Playful-Advisor-9559
comments.body: i put it on high effort to make GDD tweak changes and tell it to add stuff and then build step by step in stages

comments.author: PositiveScarcity8909
comments.body:
I start by asking Claude to make a teamplate of one after explaining my idea, then fill up the gaps and answer initial questions. After that I ask Claude to update it when I decide on new content or changes to the initial plan.

But I keep many data points and assets as placeholder with Claude guesses and modify later.

For example ability cooldowns are fully decided by Claude at this point, but I will worry about balance when I have a game to balance in the first place.

replies.author: RealNerdEthan
replies.body: This seems like a reasonable middle ground. I'll try this out.

comments.author: Lavio00
comments.body: Im frontloading design as much as possible but it is a huge, huge undertaking.

comments.author: Gugadin_
comments.body: If you writing a GDD i recommend looking into gamecollab.io and use its MCP server to make it the source of truth for you game design decisions.

comments.author: Quirky-Split7157
comments.body:
You learn this the best way by trying.

The first few times I built apps, I started with a very slim vision and built features as the ideas came. It ended up requiring a lot of work to get fixed as time went by.

Now, I try to give the AI a clear idea about the vision of the product that I am building. I try to add all sorts of ideas and rate them so my system architect (Fable) has a chance to design an optimized architecture from the get-go. From this, its much easier to build a small slice of the product to test it while having something that may scale to some of the other ideas in the backlog.

comments.author: ponderdiggums
comments.body:
GGD's are generally living documents, so you'll build on them as you go.

I start with basics - Genre/Console, Pillars, Controls, Gameplay, Inspiration/reference, Research (market share on different devices in different regions when determining min spec, for example). Then I expand as I build the game. Some folks continue to smash everything into the same massive doc, others run a library of different docs/pages (like a confluence or wiki).

comments.author: Hot-Address-6016
comments.body:
Massive GDD is a myth.  
You should make a concept and then lot of specs about different aspects.  
The GDD you’ll get from this specs at the end, not from the start.  
From the start it’s just wasting of time - many things will change many times as only you start the development.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
Build a knowledge base - big monolithic GDD’s are obsolete. Here are some docs that are far more important:

Scope document / core loop explanation  
Story/lore docs (world/characters/background)  
Concept art / mood board   
UX/UI mockups  
Level design documentation  
Prioritized backlog   
Bug database  
Tech debt doc  
Features list

replies.author: RoyalSpecialist1777
replies.body: Which are... all sections that can be in a GDD...

comments.author: Reasonable_Owl_3146
comments.body: The first version of my game I made, I had maybe a 10-page GDD, and I quickly found that time saved at first was not time saved later on. Now for version 2, I'm at a bit over 400 pages and I'm I maybe only 70% done. I'm finishing it and all the assets before I put it to code. The progress is speeding up though because the more context opus has, the better it is at reading my mind and recommending what I would want. in the last day, I'm starting to just write "approve" by half of its suggestions during the fleshing out process of my ideas.

comments.author: Nomski88
comments.body: Yes, I put together a high level master project plan that outlines the goals and steps I want to achieve. I'll then break it down into phases where I'll do dev cycles by prompting > reviewing > revising until I get the desired results. I'll then freeze it in place and move onto the next phase. It's highly effective.

comments.author: PaintingThat7623
comments.body:
The last GDD I've written for the game I'm currently working on took about 20 days about 4h each every day. It was basically the whole game written out (no specific content, say item stats for all 4000 items).

Then I've started iterating. About 20-30% of what I wanted to add had to be cut or reworked. It's normal.

BUT! The only reason I'd spent that much time on it was that I had to wait for my coworker to wrap up his project so he could join me in implementation. Otherwise I'd probabably spent 10 times less on it.

comments.author: UncleJoesLandscaping
comments.body: I have a Miro-board  with ever evolving game ideas. I also have a game description aimed at the AI to discribe the key concepts.

comments.author: RickRelentless
comments.body:
As a professional game designer, I can confidently tell you that game design and development are by definition an iterative process. You come up with a hypothesis, prototype, test, analyze outcomes, tweak, rinse repeat until things feel good. Writing out a huge GDD before you even start prototyping, waterfall style, is a rookie mistake and just wastes time.

The reason for this is simple; it is impossible to accurately predict which ideas will work well together and which ones sound great on paper, but don’t actually make your game more engaging. You need to engage with your ideas hands-on in order to vet them, and not be afraid to scrap or rework them after trying them out.

So just start with a basic one or two page GDD, that describes a high-level concept for your game, identify your one or two core mechanics and start prototyping those until they feel good, then move on from there one step at a time.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body:
Same here. It also depends on how many people are involved. Some need a strict GDD upfront, and some can't be bothered to ever read it again.

nowadays with AI I test the GDD against the game. So I can easily spot if some promised gameplay isn't implemented yet, or implemented gameplay is missing from the GDD. They keep eachother in sync now.

  
Btw, decades ago a GDD would be written and finalized before anything was made. The people writing the GDD literally finished a document and handed it off. No iteration backwards, coders just had to make what was in the GDD. Testing and iterating was a lot more difficult and costly.

replies.author: New_Patience_8107
replies.body:
Finding this out myself. Have a high level roadmap that was detailed enough but 1) doesn't capture every edge case 2)doesn't catch every feature that just isn't scalable  3) can't foresee how your scope changes.

Think your game needs a beginning and end, GDD helps that. Everything in between is clusterfuck.

replies.author: Bodyphone
replies.body:
I agree and also disagree. I think a big detailed GDD for someone making their first game is a good way to get them to think about the whole picture in a way that just prototyping wouldn’t get you. I spent a month on my GDD and it was overkill and I should have got to prototyping sooner, but I learned a lot about game development at this step that I don’t think I would have gotten if I just jumped straight into it.

Likewise there is a lot about game development I would not have learned from only writing a GDD and reading, and still a lot about game development I haven’t yet learned from either.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
It was a waste of time in the sense that you could have learned the same things a lot faster if you did it iteratively.

Like, a massive GDD doesn’t have zero value. It is just much worse than the alternatives.

replies.author: RickRelentless
replies.body:
There’s a difference between doing it as a hobbyist and doing it as a pro as well. If you went through the game design process many times, its not difficult to develop a pretty clear mental image of what the greater game is that you are working towards, and what potential complications you are likely to run in to in the future. I don’t need to write a whole bunch of stuff out in advance to discover that bit by bit anymore.

On top of that, as a pro someone pays you for your time, if they found out you spent a month writing documentation, not delivering any tangible progress in the form of playable builds that they themselves can test, you are going to be replaced very quickly.

replies.author: robhanz
replies.body:
it's good to think about the things that have to be done at a minimum to help with scope.

I've seen design docs that, printed out, were over a foot tall, both sides printer, 8 point font.  They were basically useless.

I think that a design doc can be useful, but you need to be careful about separating what you *think* will work (and needs validation) from what *actually works in the game right now*.  Those are two different things, and you need to be super careful about overly investing in something until it's proven out.

replies.author: UnderStrangeStars
replies.body:
Another fun one I see new developers doing.... they spend so much time building the big ol world... and just assume the million systems come later. 

If you want a villager that lives out a routine, you don't need a huge village built. Pick a spot on the ground, then another spot, then another spot. Build the system that they walk between those spots. Okay now you want one to do blacksmith stuff around a shop? Rig an animation separate from that villager swinging the hammer and moving around. Then you put it all together.

I've reviewed so many AI games that try to everything end to end in a prompt... I don't work with AI personally but I'm very confident it works better on a single discrete task =)

replies.author: robhanz
replies.body:
I like to think about two things in game development - ideas and facts.  Ideas are things we think will be good or work, while facts are things that we have seen.  Sometimes facts are vague and specific to one person ("Bob said this was fun"), sometimes they're of much higher quality, but they're all *seen*.  My personal opinion is that you need to invest in things in proportion to how many facts you have about them - and for pure ideas, the best thing to do is to invest the minimum you can to turn them into facts.

Where you get into problem is forward-looking design, which is often *a set of ideas that are treated like facts*.  This becomes a problem because it encourages you to invest far too heavily in things that are just speculation, and become unwilling to change them.

comments.author: ferrx
comments.body:
treat it like a backlog. "add new task: update walking animation" and it creates task-123 in your tasks MD. do this a lot, even as you're working on tasks. eventually you'll find yourself with a large backlog that provides reasonable scope far earlier in the process. 



it's how real projects work, at least in the past 15 years since Agile has taken over. you have a minimal viable product (v0.1) and then iterate with more features.. no need for a waterfall approach with every single tasks well defined.

comments.author: Tiamitsu
comments.body: Having tested both, I prefer to just do a brief summary of the project and develop it as I go. This allows for more creativity along the way and prevents you from being too constrained by a rigid structure. I also find that it works better when working with AI. That's my preferred method, and it works well for me, but I believe the other method is also valid. Try a few small projects and see what works best for you and your approach to working with AI.

comments.author: NinjaLegacyDev
comments.body: I know nothing about coding so I don’t ever see the actual code itself or do any planning prior. I tell it what system I want implemented, how I want it implemented, how it will intertwine with other systems, then I playtest and refine by being specific about changes in the next version. I repeat playtests until I’m happy with the result. I still have a long way to go with my game but I’ve made a ton of progress starting from scratch a week ago. I’m using Claude’s $20/mo plan and since it’s a 2D game with claude making all art, visuals, and animations, the file size and usage is super low. I think as of right now the games file size is just over 1mb.

comments.author: Kupke
comments.body: you cant scale the project if you dont imho, but its an illusion your gdd wont change 1000x

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
Somewhere in between works well with AI. I keep one short doc with the pillars and core loop, plus a running decisions log ("we cut X because Y") that the model reads at the start of every session. The log matters more than the GDD, because it stops the AI from cheerfully re-adding things you already tried and removed.

Detailed specs I only write for the system I'm about to build, and I rewrite that section after playtesting it. Anything further out than the next couple of systems stays as a one-line idea in a backlog, since it will almost certainly change once the earlier pieces exist.

comments.author: CMD_BLOCK
comments.body:
You will spend longer in development the more you iterate and iterate without any true design. 

You CAN do it, but things get messy, esp as the project gets bigger 

Highly recommend starting out with a very strong map and then blasting off ffom there

comments.author: SecureReindeer3989
comments.body:
As others already stated design is fluid and changes all the time so I never do more than outline the concept and feeling I'm going for. If there was a whole team that needs to move in the same direction I would use it more like an internal pitch deck.

Now I'm doing almost backwards, having AI keep my design documents updated with changes (I'm using a wiki page for this). So 2-3 Months later when I forgot why I changed something, or someone else needs to know what has already been tried we have the history for it.

comments.author: SushiMasterPro
comments.body: I am weird but I usually write small gdd then spend time in google sheets and balance it than implement. Sometimes whole gdd is sheet then I translate it for other people in team to human language

comments.author: RoyalSpecialist1777
comments.body:
Yes.  Absolutely.  With AI I prefer more waterfall style planning, with some flexibility.   People who say things will change just likely aren't as experienced in this type of pre-planning.  AI messes up way too much when things change halfway through and systems need drastic changing.  Having requirements set and finalized is so useful. But if you don't know enough about game design and architecture I can see how this would not be manageable as you are half designing things running around somewhat blind.

Will you have to tune and balance things?  Sure but ideally this won't be needed as much if you have experience and know what you want to build.

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body: Base idea, 2 handwritten papers what's actually important like multiplayer, please fantasy or workshop, rest wing

comments.author: SolrayCultist
comments.body: I didn't have one right off the bat, but I had enough of the basic core elements jotted down, with random ideas. I used Claude to organize my thoughts into a GDD that I use now. Keeps me in check with scope creep, not forgetting this or that thing in lore and whatever, and is useful for my agent to check against/refresh its "memory." On top of that it will be the perfect doc to make a game wiki or something from. If/when its all said and done.

comments.author: No-Dragonfruit-675
comments.body:
I don’t think there is a silver bullet here. As a professional you build up an intuition which allows you to quickly iterate with fewer mistakes.

Might be useful for someone who is a hobbyist to  take a step back and think things through.

comments.author: Arya_the_Gamer
comments.body:
Basically whenever I start a new project, I make an initial gdd and tell the ai to update it after every feature integration.

So it evolves.

comments.author: No-Dragonfruit-675
comments.body:
I don’t think there is a silver bullet here. As a professional you build up an intuition which allows you to quickly iterate with fewer mistakes.

Might be useful for someone who is a hobbyist to take a step back and think things through.

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body:
I'm a solo dev, so I mostly use GDD for brainstorming and inspiration.  If I know the intended design, I don't necessarily need it all documented in one place so someone else can understand it.  It can be good enough that it's in my head for the short term.

With AI coding agents I work iteratively, architecting and designing one sub-system with the AI piece by piece.  So far this has worked well in the early build phase where I'm more just building the foundational systems into the game rather than populating content or play arcs.  I'll likely have to transition to a system that works towards pre-defined milestones rather than building whatever is interesting next once there is enough meat on the bones for the game to start being interesting to players.  Otherwise scope creep will probably kill me.

I also separate technical architecture/design from design which is more narrative.  While they do interact, it's easier to think through problems in one or the other space without clutter from the other.  Especially with AI agents who will misread proposed character traits of an NPC as implementation requirements.

comments.author: algorys
comments.body:
I have a general vision, as well as specific ideas regarding game mechanics, the atmosphere, and the genre.

But beyond that, I iterate and run tests. Sometimes you come up with a game mechanic, only to realize it doesn't quite work. So, you try something else or find a different way to implement that feature.

If you could have seen the first version, you’d realize it looks nothing like what it is today! xD

comments.author: lordpoee
comments.body: I do a roadmap, a game bible  and an asset manifest and this reduces the number iterations but there will always be later iterations.

comments.author: Suspicious_Bet3623
comments.body: GDDs are essential if you're prone to losing focus or feature creep.  Lay out your ideas, make sure all the base mechanics are mapped out, and most importantly why the game is going to be entertaining.

comments.author: count023
comments.body:
GDD first, come up with a skeleto of hte mechanics and the gameplay i want to crib, ideally with refernces frm other games. Once i have that, flesh it out more to at least break down teh game structure into modules and such then start building modules in a self contained state with entry points and exit points for how they link to other modules. 

  
The GDD is a must, it's basically the same as just doing plan mode at the start of te project, except it also helps fiht off scope creep and give sthe AI an consistent skeleton of structure to refer back to when building out components. 

  
A giant GDD out of the gate, that's silly, it's not needed, but a general structure of what you attempt to accomplish, 100%, and then you refine it as you go and prototype out features and the like.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
What even is a GDD? Never heard of this before AI came along.

I build iteratively. I have a vision, a bunch of chaotic design documents, some roadmap for specific initiatives, specs and plans for individual feature increments.

And I playtest each increment. Because I care about my game being playable and fun. I'm not interested in making something that only looks good so I can show it off.

replies.author: Ill_Contest_535
replies.body:

really?

comments.author: _agge_
comments.body: build build build build

comments.author: MidSerpent
comments.body:
No. 

Most of a massive GDD is going to be wasted effort. 

I make lots of little documents

comments.author: Ill_Contest_535
comments.body:
what about GDD/document style prompting?

does that work for the AI?

comments.author: azicre
comments.body: Most good harness' these days include a gdd/documentation md.

comments.author: BadassMinh
comments.body: I write down all my ideas, feed it to AI and discuss with it exactly my desired mechanics. Then have it write down a big GDD and have it code everything. With any changes that deviate from the original document are all noted down there. It isn't meant to be a document I keep updating but just for something for AI to read and follow it without me having to iterate every steps. My most recent one the coders have been working for about 1 month straight now (I know I'm probably doing something  wrong lol)
